deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the previous page): the heading is 'Verallgemeinerung des Cauchyschen Satzes ... auf 2 complexe Variable'. An irreducible algebraic surface S: f(x,y,z)=0 is given. Two 'functions of the Gebilde' are chosen, i.e. rational functions phi, psi in C(x,y,z) restricted to S. These are algebraic functions of two of the variables, say x and y.

The page defines and states the following.

(1) Local multiplicity. Fix values a, b and a point P=(alpha,beta,gamma) on S with phi(P)=a and psi(P)=b. Consider the algebraic curve C_a = S ∩ {phi - a = 0}. Restrict psi to C_a and regard it as an algebraic function of x alone. Suppose psi takes the value b at P exactly m times, i.e. ord_P(psi - b | C_a) = m. Then one says the pair (phi, psi) takes the value pair (a,b) exactly m times at P.
- Modern form (where P is a smooth point and the curves have no common component): m = i_P(phi - a, psi - b) = dim_C O_{S,P}/(phi - a, psi - b).
- My addition: for this to be correct, the order must be measured in a local uniformizer of each branch of C_a through P, summed over branches. It should not be measured in x itself where x ramifies.

(2) Symmetry. The same integer m equals the number of times phi, restricted to C'_b = S ∩ {psi - b = 0} and viewed as a function of x, takes the value a at P. That is, ord_P(psi - b | C_a) = ord_P(phi - a | C'_b). This is the symmetry of the local intersection multiplicity.

(3) Invariance. m does not depend on which of x, y, z is taken as the independent variable. This holds once orders are taken with respect to branch uniformizers (my gloss).

(4) A crossed-out sentence begins a further characterisation of m at the point (alpha,beta,gamma) but is abandoned.

(5) 'Two theorems hold'. Only the first is stated.
- Theorem 1: on f=0 the pair (phi, psi) takes every value pair (a,b) equally often in total (counted with the multiplicity m above). In particular it takes (0,0) as often as 'infinity'.
- In modern terms: the total count sum_{P in (phi,psi)^{-1}(a,b)} i_P equals the degree of the generically finite rational map (phi,psi): S --> P^2 (or P^1 x P^1). This is the 2-dimensional analogue of the curve theorem that a rational function on a compact Riemann surface has as many zeros as poles: the argument principle / Cauchy, Riemann.

(6) Further remarks.
- 'Relations to ideal theory': the multiplicities are lengths of quotients by the ideal (phi - a, psi - b), in the spirit of Kronecker, Noether and Hilbert's own ideal theory.
- The 'Unbestimmtheitscurven' (curves of indeterminacy, where phi or psi has the form 0/0) deserve special attention. The last line, only partly legible, seems to say they have no zero point(s) [reading uncertain].

No computation is carried out. The page is a definition plus statements, apparently notebook or lecture-planning material.
errors: The multiplicity is defined via 'psi as an algebraic function of x alone'. Literally taken, the order in x is wrong where x ramifies along C_a at P, or where P is a singular point of C_a. The order must be taken in branch uniformizers and summed over branches. The invariance claim in (3) is only true with that reading.

The definition presupposes that phi - a and psi - b have no common curve component through P and that P is not an indeterminacy point of phi or psi. Otherwise m is infinite or undefined; the remark on Unbestimmtheitscurven acknowledges this only afterwards.

Theorem 1 ('every value pair equally often') holds only for value pairs whose fibre is finite. For special (a,b) the fibre can be a whole curve (contracted curves of the map). Indeterminacy (base) points must be excluded or blown up.

'Equally often 0 and equally often infinity' is ambiguous for a pair of functions. Typically the polar loci of phi and psi are curves meeting each other and the base locus, so (infinity, infinity) can occur along curves or at base points. As stated, the claim needs a projective compactification and conventions; it is not justified on the page.
The page announces 'Es gelten nun 2 Sätze' but states only one; the second theorem is missing.
Symmetry ord(psi - b | C_a) = ord(phi - a | C'_b) is correct at smooth points of S (more generally at Cohen–Macaulay points). It is asserted without proof.

results.what: Definition of the multiplicity with which two functions on an algebraic surface take a value pair at a point, via the order of one function restricted to a level curve of the other
results.modern_name: local intersection multiplicity i_P(phi-a, psi-b) = length O_{S,P}/(phi-a, psi-b)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Cayley, Noether, Halphen for plane curves); rigorous algebraic theory by Severi, van der Waerden, Weil (1920s-40s)

results.what: Symmetry: order of psi-b on curve phi=a equals order of phi-a on curve psi=b; independence from the choice of independent variable
results.modern_name: symmetry of intersection multiplicity of two curves on a surface

results.what: Theorem: a pair of rational functions on an algebraic surface takes every value pair equally often in total (generalisation of 'as many zeros as poles' from curves)
results.modern_name: constancy of fibre cardinality (with multiplicity) = degree of a generically finite rational map S -> P^2; conservation of number
results.usually_credited_to: Analogue of Cauchy/Riemann for curves; for two variables Kronecker (characteristic, 1869), Picard–Simart, Noether; rigorous form 20th c.

results.what: Remark that curves of indeterminacy (base loci) require special treatment and link with ideal theory
results.modern_name: base locus / indeterminacy of rational maps; resolution by blow-up; ideal-theoretic multiplicity

deep.surprise_reason: This is a sketch of standard 19th-century material: the two-variable analogue of the zeros-equal-poles theorem and local intersection multiplicity, of the kind found in Picard–Simart and Noether. The ideal-theoretic remark fits Hilbert's known interests. Nothing goes beyond what was known at the time, and the statements are imprecise about indeterminacy and infinity.
